title: Ekuru
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Plain peeled beans blended semi-smooth and beaten ten to fifteen minutes with a mixer — or thirty by hand — until very fluffy, then steamed to a crumble.
longDesc: Ekuru is moin moin with everything taken out. No peppers, no oil, no fish, no seasoning in the batter at all — just peeled beans, blended deliberately not-too-smooth and then worked until they are frothy. The target texture is crumbly, and that is entirely a function of how much air you beat in: under-aerate and you get moin moin texture or hard ekuru, which is the author's own warning. The pepper and the oil live in a separate sauce eaten with it, either ata dindin or ebatu.
ingredients: Banana leaves (moin moin leaves), ramekins, or foil
equipment: Hand mixer, or a wooden spoon or ladle
steps: Blend with a little water till semi-smooth — that is, not too smooth.
Mix with a hand mixer 10 to 15 minutes until very fluffy and frothy. With a wooden spoon or ladle instead, mix for 30 minutes.
Scoop the batter into banana leaves, ramekins or foil and seal.
Steam till fully cooked, roughly 30 minutes on medium heat.
Serve crumbled, with ata dindin (NGA026) or ebatu (NGA027).
chefTips: Semi-smooth, not smooth. This is the opposite target from moin moin, where the author blends very fine and frothy. The slightly coarser grind is part of what gives ekuru its crumble.
Ten to fifteen minutes with a mixer, thirty by hand. Ekuru gets more beating than any other bean dish in the repertoire and that is the point.
No salt in the batter. The author's own ingredient list mentions salt but the method never adds it — the seasoning comes entirely from the sauce.
The failure mode is stated plainly: if the batter is not fluffy enough you end up with moin moin texture, or hard ekuru.
Eaten with the hands. Crumble it, spoon the sauce over, mix it on the plate, and the author's line is worth quoting — 'so starts forming "Butter"'.
Ramekins work but leaves are better. The leaf is the only flavour this dish gets from its wrapper.
If you are making ebatu, the vegetables steam in the same pot alongside the ekuru for the first fifteen minutes.
commonMistakes: Seasoning the batter, which makes it moin moin.
Steaming submerged rather than above the water.
Serving it whole in a slab instead of crumbled.
sources: Adapted from 'Ekuru And Ata Dindin (Fried Stew)', byline Sisi Jemimah. The ekuru method is verbatim in substance: 'First soak and peel your Beans. Then blend with little water till semi-smooth, that's not too smooth'; mix with a hand mixer 10 to 15 minutes until 'very fluffy and frothy', or 'you can use a wooden spoon or ladle, mix for 30 minutes'; scoop into banana leaves, ramekins or foil; 'Steam till fully cooked, this should take roughly 30 minutes on medium heat.' Bean quantity as printed: 3 cups black-eyed or brown.

THE DISTINCTION FROM MOIN MOIN, answered by the one author who published both, verbatim: 'Ekuru is made from steamed blended dehulled beans, it is a tad bit similar to Moinmoin.' And the operative part: 'You'll need to work your batter really well to achieve the signature Ekuru crumbly texture. If your batter isn't fluffy enough, you'll end up with a Moinmoin type texture or hard Ekuru.' So the difference is aeration and seasoning, not the ingredient list.
Note the opposite blending targets within her own work: ekuru 'semi-smooth, that's not too smooth'; moin moin 'very fine and frothy' with no lumps (NGA022).

STRUCTURAL FLAG on the source page: the ingredient list is headed 'Ekuru' but everything after the beans belongs to the sauce, and those items are then re-listed separately under Ata Dindin. The ekuru method uses only the beans. The list is mis-sectioned on the page, and only the beans are carried over here.
LISTED BUT NEVER USED: 'Salt to taste' appears in the batter list and the batter is never salted in the method. Recorded rather than corrected.
Her serving note, verbatim: 'Ekuru is eaten with your hands oh, so starts forming "Butter." Crumble up your Ekuru, add the sauce, mix thoroughly, wash your hand and dig in!'
1Q Food Platter's ekuru page describes it as 'simply ground beans, wrapped and steamed' but does NOT quantify the ekuru itself — only its ebatu sauce (NGA027).
reheating: Steam 10 minutes. It firms up cold and softens again with steam.
healthBenefits: Entirely oil-free as cooked — the fat is all in the sauce beside it.
High in plant protein, folate and soluble fibre.
Vegan and gluten-free on its own.
culturalNote: Ekuru is the plainest thing in the Yoruba repertoire and it exists to carry a sauce. That separation — bland steamed protein on one side, a fiercely fried pepper sauce on the other, combined by the eater — is a recurring shape in Yoruba cooking, and it is the same logic as ewa agoyin, where plain mashed beans meet a dark pepper sauce made separately.
